basics.name: thisTOthat (This to That: Glue Advice), the 'glue this to that' material-pair glue selector
basics.url: https://www.thistothat.com/ (home page with the two drop-down menus; opened). Example result page: https://www.thistothat.com/cgi-bin/glue.cgi?this=Wood&that=Plastic (opened). Selection philosophy: https://www.thistothat.com/phil.shtml (opened)
basics.resource_type: interactive tool (a web 'glue calculator': pick material A and material B from two drop-down menus, get a results page of recommended glues), plus short glue-type explainer pages
basics.cost: Free, no account. Paid for by advertising (Google AdSense code is in every page); the site has a Statement of Impartiality saying advertisers don't influence its picks
basics.license: All rights reserved ('Copyright © 1999-2024 thistothat.com, All rights reserved' in the page footer). No open licence, so link to it but don't copy its text, tables or icons. The pairing facts (e.g. 'for wood to plastic they suggest a silicone-type glue, then 5-minute epoxy, then contact cement') can be summarised in our own words with a citation
basics.language: English, with a French interface (index_fr.shtml, 'Attachez (Ceci) à (Cela)'); how much of the results and glue pages are translated into French was not checked [uncertain]
basics.year: Launched 1999 (copyright line '1999-...'; the 'Glue of the Month' archive runs from the early 2000s to August 2003). Restyled for mobile phones on 2 November 2018 (News page). Latest news item seen: 20 March 2025. Home page footer reads 1999-2024; results pages read 1999-2023
basics.image_license: All rights reserved. The site has almost no pictures: small icons (tip, toxicity, time, link) only, and no photos or diagrams of joints
basics.authority_level: community or unvetted: an independent hobby/consumer advice site run by a small team (the Links page cross-links other sites 'also by us', e.g. Hogdex, a Toronto portal). Recommendations come from the authors' own household tests plus manufacturers' safety data sheets (MSDS) for toxicity ratings; no named experts or references

coverage.covers: Adhesive bonding only, for common household materials. 11 materials in each menu: ceramic, fabric, glass, leather, metal, paper, plastic, rubber, Styrofoam (expanded polystyrene foam), vinyl and wood, which gives 66 different material pairs (121 ordered choices; 'A to B' and 'B to A' give the same advice). All 66 pairs were opened and all return a recommendation. Across them the results link about 45 glue pages: roughly 10 generic glue-type pages (cyanoacrylate, PVA, contact adhesive, spray adhesive, hot glue, silicone-based glue, metal epoxy, PVC adhesive, plus 'reactivity' and 'clamping' tip pages) and about 35 named consumer products (mostly Canadian/US brands). The FAQ says the site deliberately sticks to 'common household items' and has no concrete, stone or skin advice
coverage.organisation: A two-question decision tool: 'Attach (This) to (That)'. The answer page lists glues in ranked or conditional groups: 'For the strongest bond…', 'For a faster bond, but not as foolproof…', 'For a less toxic alternative…', 'If appearance isn't much of a concern…', 'If you want the joint to stay flexible…', 'If your vinyl has a woven back…', 'If you are gluing PVC plumbing pipes…'. Tip notes follow (clean metal with steel wool, glass must be oil-free, test plastics in a hidden spot, sand glossy plastic with 120 grit, never put solvent glue or hot glue straight onto Styrofoam). Each product links to a page naming its glue family and giving toxicity icons and setting time. This works very well for someone with no vocabulary: you only need to know the names of the two materials
coverage.scope_match: medium: it's exactly the beginner 'which glue for these two materials' question the project wants for its adhesive family, and it's a model for the flow-chart UX. But it answers with brand products rather than adhesive types, covers only 11 coarse materials (all plastics are one bucket), and covers nothing else in the project's scope (no mechanisms or mechanical connections)
coverage.taxonomy_used: A material × material grid (11 × 11, symmetric), not a chemistry taxonomy. Each recommended product is tagged with a glue family on its own page (e.g. 'This is a contact adhesive', 'This is a flexible PVA', 'This is a metal epoxy', 'This is a cyanoacrylate', 'This is a silicone-based glue', 'This is a spray adhesive'). Material groups are the everyday names: 11 top-level materials with no sub-types (e.g. no ABS vs PLA vs polypropylene split)
coverage.example_types: Types it recommends or explains (by type, not brand): cyanoacrylate (superglue/instant glue), gap-filling thicker cyanoacrylate, two-part epoxy (5-minute and regular cure), metal-filled epoxy (the 'metal epoxy' family, e.g. J-B Weld type) and epoxy putty for gaps, contact adhesive / contact cement (solvent-based and water-based 'green' versions), spray adhesive (spray-on contact adhesive, including a rubber-to-rubber grade), PVA white glue and yellow carpenter's glue (polyvinyl acetate), flexible PVA (fabric and bookbinding glues), hot-melt glue (glue gun), 'silicone-based' flexible glue (the Goop/E6000 family, which the site calls silicone-based; other sources call these solvent-based rubbery (elastomeric) adhesives [uncertain]), UV-curing glass glue (light-cure adhesive that sets in sunlight), PVC pipe cement (solvent cement; the site wrongly calls it anaerobic), starch paste (rice-starch paper paste), moisture-curing polyurethane glue (one product), construction adhesive (caulking-tube panel adhesive), and solvent-resistant solvent-based clear glue
coverage.making_methods: Household repairs, crafts, sewing and upholstery, bookbinding and paper craft, theatre props and costumes, light woodwork. Not aimed at 3D printing, CNC or robotics, and doesn't mention printed plastics such as PLA, PETG or ABS
coverage.item_count: 11 materials; 66 unique material pairs (all with advice); about 45 linked glue pages (about 10 generic type or tip pages plus about 35 products); about 30 archived 'Glue of the Month' reviews
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Adhesive types only. It covers cyanoacrylate, two-part epoxy, metal epoxy/epoxy putty, contact cement, spray adhesive, PVA (rigid and flexible), hot melt, silicone-type flexible glue, UV-curing glass glue, PVC solvent cement, starch paste and polyurethane, and matches them to ceramic, fabric, glass, leather, metal, paper, plastic, rubber, polystyrene foam, vinyl and wood. The other special behaviours (torque-limiting, self-locking, hand-release, one-way/ratchet, indexing, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors) are not covered. It does touch on 'flexible vs stiff joint' as a selection factor (flexible PVA or silicone-type glue when the joint must bend)
coverage.entry_structure: Results page: heading 'Material A to Material B', 1 to 5 ranked or conditional recommendation groups, each with 1 to 4 product links, then tip notes. Product page: glue family ('This is a contact adhesive'), a short comment, toxicity icons for inhalation, ingestion and skin absorption (3 levels each, taken from MSDS), time to adhere, where to buy, related products and a link to the maker. Generic type page (e.g. cyanoacrylate, PVA, contact, hot glue): a paragraph plus a bulleted list of how-to tips
coverage.audience_level: hobbyist (general public, crafters, DIY home repair)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: high: two plain drop-downs, everyday material names, humorous plain-English writing, clear 'strongest / fastest / least toxic / most invisible' trade-off labels, and practical tips (clamp it, sand it, clean it, test in a hidden spot). Downsides: answers are brand names that may not be sold outside Canada or the US, and some chemistry explanations are wrong (see gaps)
usefulness.has_images: Barely: only small icons (tip, toxicity level, time). No photos or diagrams of joints, glue application or failure modes
usefulness.gaps: (1) Answers are brand products, many of them Canadian (LePage's) or discontinued (e.g. Loctite 349 Impruv 'has been replaced'), so readers must work back to the adhesive type. (2) Only 11 coarse materials: 'plastic' is one bucket, so it can't handle hard-to-glue plastics (polyethylene, polypropylene, PTFE; low surface energy) versus easy ones, and says only 'there are so many kinds of plastic… try a small test'. No 3D-printed plastics, foam board, cork, stone, concrete or composites. (3) Some technical errors: it says cyanoacrylate sets 'through the evaporation process' (it actually sets by reacting with surface moisture: anionic polymerisation), calls PVC pipe cement 'anaerobic' (it's a solvent cement that softens and fuses the pipe), and calls Goop/E6000 'silicone-based' [uncertain]. (4) No numbers: no gap sizes, strengths, temperature ranges or cure times beyond a few 'time to adhere' values. (5) Nothing on joint design (lap vs butt, peel vs shear) beyond the philosophy page's 'more surface area is stronger' and 'combine glue with a screw, nail or stitching'. (6) No waterproof, outdoor, heat or food-safe filter. (7) Little updating since the 2000s
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Yes. Result pages have stable query URLs per material pair, e.g. https://www.thistothat.com/cgi-bin/glue.cgi?this=Wood&that=Plastic and https://www.thistothat.com/cgi-bin/glue.cgi?this=Metal&that=Glass, and glue-type pages have stable .shtml URLs (e.g. https://www.thistothat.com/glue/cyan.shtml for cyanoacrylate, https://www.thistothat.com/glue/pva.shtml for PVA, https://www.thistothat.com/glue/contact.shtml for contact adhesive; all opened). Best used as a 'try it yourself' link from adhesive entries
usefulness.reusable_data: Scrape-only (plain server-rendered HTML from a simple CGI script; there's no API or download). The 11 × 11 grid is small enough to summarise by hand. All rights reserved, so the grid and wording can't be copied or republished; only facts restated in our own words with a citation
usefulness.maintained: Online and working in September 2026: all 66 pairs return results. Lightly maintained: mobile restyle in 2018, news items up to March 2025, footer copyright 2024. Glue of the Month stopped in 2003 ('Sorry about missing a few months of updates'). Many product recommendations are old, and some are commented out or replaced in the page source. Wayback Machine history couldn't be checked from this environment [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) The two-drop-down 'Attach THIS to THAT' entry point is the ideal first step for the adhesive branch of the flow chart: people know their materials, not chemistry names. (2) A symmetric material × material grid (every pair has an answer) as the adhesive data model, but with adhesive TYPES as answers and finer material classes (e.g. split plastics into 'easy to glue' vs 'slippery/low surface energy: PE, PP'). (3) Ranked answer groups labelled by the trade-off: strongest / fastest / least toxic / most invisible / stays flexible / fills gaps. (4) Conditional follow-up questions inside a result ('Does your vinyl have a woven back?', 'Is it PVC plumbing pipe?', 'Is the glass clear enough for UV light?'). (5) Per-material 'gotcha' tips (e.g. solvent glue melts polystyrene foam; put hot glue on the other part first and let it cool a few seconds; sand glossy plastic; clean metal). (6) A simple 3-level toxicity rating for breathing, swallowing and skin contact. (7) The philosophy page's beginner rules: no glue is universal, the glue must suit the material, the bond is only as strong as the weakest material, more surface area means a stronger bond, and add a mechanical fastener where possible
usefulness.design_rules_given: Almost none. Only qualitative rules (more area = stronger, clamp PVA, use two coats of contact cement on porous materials, bond contact cement within about 2 hours, sand plastic with 120 grit). A few 'time to adhere' figures (e.g. hot glue fast, PVC adhesive 3 hours, metal epoxy 4 to 6 hours). No gap sizes, strengths or temperature limits
usefulness.terminology_value: low to medium: good for everyday names (superglue, white glue, contact cement, hot glue, spray adhesive, epoxy putty) and a few terms (adherend, contact adhesive, cyanoacrylate, PVA). Not an authority, because some chemistry descriptions are wrong
usefulness.decision_support: Yes, and it's the core of the site: a two-input selector (material A × material B from 11 choices each) returning ranked and conditional recommendations with trade-off labels (strength, speed, toxicity, visibility, flexibility, large-area use) and per-material tips. The logic is a hand-written lookup table (one CGI script, one answer per pair), with no weighting or filtering by environment (heat, water, outdoor)
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Original content based on the authors' own tests and manufacturers' MSDS sheets. Similar 'glue this to that' tools exist (e.g. manufacturers' consumer glue advisers such as Loctite's consumer 'Product Advisor' and gluing guides, which recommend only their own brand). Overlaps in purpose with the manufacturers' technical selection tables (Henkel Loctite, 3M, Permabond: chemistry × substrate ratings), which are more authoritative but less beginner-friendly. Reviewed approvingly by Kevin Kelly's Cool Tools (2004: 'functions as a glue calculator… pretty reliable') and Improvised Life (2022: 'may not be up-to-date with the latest in glue technology')
